summary: A comparative analysis of nature spirit folklore in rural Ireland (the Sidhe) and the Andes (Pachamama and the Apus), based on interviews with storytellers, a farmer, an anthropologist, an elder and a historian. It argues that geography shapes the form of the spirits, that the lore influences agriculture and acts as informal environmental conservation, and that storytelling and new heritage institutions help preserve it against modern pressures like social media dilution.
one_line: Comparison of Irish Sidhe and Andean Pachamama/Apu spirit lore, showing how geography shapes myths and how they guide agriculture and conservation.
key_facts: The author arrived in rural western Ireland on a misty September morning in 2023.

Storyteller Aiden O'Sullivan says the Sidhe, associated with ancient mounds or fairy forts, are 'the stewards of the natural world' and that cutting an old tree or disturbing a fort invites misfortune on yourself and your crops.
Farmer Mairead Collins recalls her grandfather always leaving an offering at the base of the Hawthorn tree to honor the spirits.
Irish lore also includes banshees and protective water creatures like the selkies.
In the Andes, Pachamama is revered as the earth mother and the Apus as protecting spirits of the mountains, about 10,000 kilometers from Ireland.
Ecuadorian anthropologist Lucia Gomez describes Apus as intermediaries between our world and the cosmos, providing guidance and protection.
Elder Don Carlos Mamani says ceremonies are performed each planting and harvest season to thank Pachamama and the Apus, and that 'When the volcano rumbles... it's the Apu speaking.'
Historian Dr. Fiona Byrne, interviewed on October 15, 2023, argues geography dictates the form of nature spirits: elusive, landmark-tied Sidhe in Ireland versus towering, overt Apus in the Andes.
In Ireland, agricultural activities may avoid certain days believed to belong to the Sidhe, while in the Andes rituals and offerings mark the agricultural calendar.
Fear of disrupting the Sidhe or angering the Apus works as a form of conservation, making both regions reluctant to alter landscapes drastically.
Dr. Byrne says digitization helps share and preserve stories but risks diluting their potency, as social media lets tales travel disconnected from their origins.
The Sidhe Heritage Centre opened in Ireland on June 12, 2024.
The Andean Spirits Institute was founded in Ecuador on August 21, 2024.
The note concludes that geography molds myths but humanity's reverence for nature is universal.
